rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.solution:
The equilibrium exists in BASIC MEDIUM.

Written out with the species that actually take part, the change is
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{OH^-} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Hydroxide ions are CONSUMED going forwards, so supplying them — that is, making the medium basic — drives the equilibrium to the right and the orange dichromate turns to yellow chromate.

Acid does the opposite. Adding \(\mathrm{H^+}\) removes hydroxide, pulls the equilibrium back, and the orange returns:
\(2\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Note that this is a pH-controlled equilibrium, NOT a redox change: chromium stays at \(+6\) throughout, and only the way the oxygens are shared alters.

rows.stem: Which of the following is the strongest acid ?
rows.solution:
The strongest acid is p-NITROBENZOIC ACID, \(p\)-\(\mathrm{O_2N{-}C_6H_4COOH}\).

The acidity of a substituted benzoic acid is decided by what the substituent does to the CARBOXYLATE ion left behind after the proton leaves. An electron-WITHDRAWING group helps disperse the negative charge, stabilises the anion, and makes the acid stronger; an electron-RELEASING group does the reverse.

The nitro group is the most strongly electron withdrawing of those offered — it withdraws both inductively and by resonance — so it gives the strongest acid.

Chlorine withdraws inductively but donates weakly by resonance, so p-chlorobenzoic acid is only modestly stronger than benzoic acid itself. The hydroxyl group is electron RELEASING by resonance, so p-hydroxybenzoic acid is the WEAKEST of the four, and unsubstituted benzoic acid sits between them.

Maltose is made up of GLUCOSE AND GLUCOSE — two units of the same sugar.

The two are joined by a glycosidic linkage between \(\mathrm{C_1}\) of the first and \(\mathrm{C_4}\) of the second. That leaves the SECOND unit's anomeric carbon free, so it can open to the straight-chain form and expose an aldehyde group — which is why maltose is a REDUCING sugar.

The other options name other disaccharides. Glucose with fructose is SUCROSE, and glucose with galactose is LACTOSE. Sucrose is the one non-reducing member of the three, because there the linkage runs between the anomeric carbons of BOTH units and neither ring can open.

rows.stem: The system that forms maximum boiling azeotrope is :
rows.solution:
CHLOROFORM AND ACETONE form a maximum boiling azeotrope.

A maximum boiling azeotrope requires a NEGATIVE deviation from Raoult's law — a vapour pressure lower than predicted, and so a boiling point higher than either pure component.

Chloroform and acetone give exactly that. Neither liquid hydrogen bonds to itself, but mixing them creates a NEW hydrogen bond: the chloroform hydrogen, made acidic by its three chlorines, bonds to the lone pair on the acetone oxygen. Unlike molecules therefore attract one another more strongly than like ones, and the escaping tendency falls.

The other systems go the other way or nowhere. Carbon disulphide with acetone and ethanol with acetone both show POSITIVE deviations and form MINIMUM boiling azeotropes. Benzene and toluene are so alike chemically that they form a nearly IDEAL solution and no azeotrope at all.

rows.stem: A zero-order reaction is one whose rate is independent of :
rows.solution:
A zero-order reaction has a rate independent of the CONCENTRATION OF THE REACTANT.

That is precisely what the order zero means: in \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^0\) the concentration term becomes 1, so
\(\text{Rate} = k\)
and the reaction proceeds at a steady rate until the reactant runs out.

Such behaviour is usually the mark of a surface-catalysed reaction. The decomposition of ammonia on a hot platinum surface is the standard example: the surface is already saturated, so adding more ammonia gives it nowhere to go and changes nothing.

Temperature is the trap. NO reaction is independent of temperature — the rate constant itself obeys the Arrhenius equation and rises steeply with it, zero-order reactions included.

rows.stem: Which of the following is most reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reaction ?

options.label: A
options.text: Chlorobenzene (drawn as a Kekule benzene hexagon bearing \(\mathrm{Cl}\))

rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — only option (A) is drawn; (B), (C) and (D) are printed as ordinary condensed formulae. Read at 5x, the drawing is a hexagon with THREE inner double-bond lines (a Kekule benzene ring, NOT a plain cyclohexane hexagon) carrying \(\mathrm{Cl}\) on a ring carbon, i.e. chlorobenzene. Naming it is a lossless reading and cannot leak the answer, which is a different option, so the row is answerable from the text above; the crop is still worth attaching. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The most reactive is the ALLYLIC chloride, \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}CH_2{-}Cl}\).

Its chlorine sits on an \(sp^3\) carbon NEXT TO the double bond, so the carbocation left behind when the chloride departs is delocalised over two carbons by resonance. An easily formed, well-stabilised cation means a fast substitution.

The other three all have something against them. n-Propyl chloride is an ordinary primary halide with no such stabilisation. Vinyl chloride is the OPPOSITE case to the allylic one: its chlorine is attached directly TO a doubly bonded carbon, its lone pair is fed into the double bond, the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond gains partial double bond character, and it is extremely unreactive. Chlorobenzene is unreactive for the same reason, with the ring in place of the double bond.

The lesson is that a double bond NEXT TO the halogen helps enormously, while a double bond AT the halogen hinders almost absolutely.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
The product (X) obtained in the following reaction is :
A cyclohexane ring carrying \(\mathrm{=O}\) on one ring carbon and \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) on the ring carbon para to it, treated with \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+OH^-}\), gives (X).

options.label: A
options.text: A cyclohexane ring carrying \(\mathrm{-OH}\) on one ring carbon and \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) on the ring carbon para to it

options.label: B
options.text: A cyclohexane ring carrying \(\mathrm{=O}\) on one ring carbon and \(\mathrm{-COO^-}\) on the ring carbon para to it

options.label: C
options.text: A cyclohexane ring carrying \(\mathrm{=O}\) on one ring carbon and \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\) on the ring carbon para to it

options.label: D
options.text: A cyclohexane ring carrying \(\mathrm{-OH}\) on one ring carbon and \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\) on the ring carbon para to it

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the reactant AND all four options are drawn skeletal structures; the stem names nothing, so the drawings ARE the question. Read at 5x: every one of the five rings is a PLAIN hexagon with no inner lines (saturated cyclohexane, NOT benzene — checked deliberately, since this corpus distinguishes the two), and in every one the two substituents sit on opposite (1,4 / para) vertices, the upper one drawn at the top vertex and the lower one hanging from the bottom vertex. The reactant carries \(\mathrm{=O}\) over \(\mathrm{CHO}\); (A) \(\mathrm{OH}\) over \(\mathrm{CHO}\); (B) \(\mathrm{=O}\) over \(\mathrm{COO^-}\); (C) \(\mathrm{=O}\) over \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\); (D) \(\mathrm{OH}\) over \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\). The option texts describe the ring and its substituent positions rather than giving IUPAC names, which is lossless and keeps the four alternatives distinguishable in text; the crop should still be attached. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
Tollens' reagent is a MILD oxidising agent, and it is selective: it oxidises an ALDEHYDE and leaves a KETONE alone.

The substrate carries both — an aldehyde group on one ring carbon and a ketone on the carbon para to it. So only the aldehyde is attacked, and since the reagent is alkaline the product is the CARBOXYLATE ion rather than the free acid.

Product: the ring still carrying its \(\mathrm{{=}O}\), with the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) now a \(-\mathrm{COO^-}\) on the carbon para to it.

The other options all involve REDUCTION — of the aldehyde, of the ketone, or of both — and Tollens' reagent is an oxidising agent, so none of them is possible. The selectivity is the whole point: a ketone has no hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon to be removed, which is why it survives.

rows.stem: Which of the following has the highest boiling point ?
rows.solution:
ETHANOIC ACID, \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\), has the highest boiling point.

Boiling point tracks the strength of the intermolecular forces, and only one of these four can hydrogen bond to itself — the acid, whose hydrogen sits on oxygen.

More than that, a carboxylic acid forms a DIMER: two molecules join through TWO hydrogen bonds at once, each one's \(\mathrm{O-H}\) reaching the other's carbonyl oxygen. The species that must be vaporised is effectively twice the size, which is why ethanoic acid boils at 391 K while acetone, of similar mass, boils at 329 K.

Ethanal and acetone have only dipole-dipole forces, and ethanoyl chloride likewise. None of the three has a hydrogen on an electronegative atom to donate.

rows.stem: Phenol does not undergo nucleophilic substitution reaction easily due to :

options.label: A
options.text: Partial double bond character of C – OH bond

options.label: B
options.text: Partial double bond character of C – C bond

rows.solution:
Because the \(\mathrm{C-OH}\) bond in phenol has PARTIAL DOUBLE BOND CHARACTER.

The oxygen's lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, and one consequence is that electron density is pushed back into the carbon-oxygen bond. That bond becomes shorter and stronger — partly a double bond — and a bond with double bond character does not break to let a nucleophile substitute for the hydroxyl group.

A second reason, not among the options, points the same way: the carbon carrying the hydroxyl is \(sp^2\) hybridised, which holds the shared pair more tightly than an \(sp^3\) carbon would.

The acidic nature of phenol is a real property but the wrong explanation: it concerns breaking the \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond, whereas substitution requires breaking the \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond. And the phenoxide ion is unusually STABLE, not unstable — which is exactly why phenol is acidic.

rows.stem: The suitable Grignard reagent used for the synthesis of \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-OH}\) with methanal is :
rows.solution:
The reagent is ISOPROPYLMAGNESIUM BROMIDE, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHMgBr}\).

Work backwards from the product. A Grignard reagent adds to a carbonyl carbon, and with METHANAL — the only aldehyde carrying two hydrogens there — the product after hydrolysis is a PRIMARY alcohol with one carbon MORE than the reagent:
\(\mathrm{R{-}MgBr} + \mathrm{HCHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{R{-}CH_2OH}\)

The target is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH{-}CH_2{-}OH}\), so \(\mathrm{R{-}CH_2OH}\) with \(\mathrm{R} = \mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH{-}}\). The reagent must therefore be the isopropyl one.

The isobutyl reagent offered as a distractor already HAS the four-carbon skeleton, so it would give a five-carbon alcohol. Methanal always adds exactly one carbon, which is what makes the arithmetic here decisive.

All proteins on hydrolysis give \(\alpha\)-AMINO ACIDS.

A protein is a polymer of amino acid residues joined by peptide bonds, and hydrolysis breaks every one of those bonds, returning the residues to the free acids they came from. They are all \(\alpha\)-amino acids — the amino group on the carbon ADJACENT to the carboxyl — which is a defining feature of proteins.

POLYPEPTIDES are the trap: they are what PARTIAL hydrolysis gives, an intermediate stage on the way down. Complete hydrolysis goes past them to the individual acids.

Enzymes are themselves proteins, not hydrolysis products, and glucose comes from a carbohydrate, not a protein.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Fluoroacetic acid is stronger acid than chloroacetic acid.
Reason (R) : This is due to greater electron withdrawing nature of F than Cl.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Fluoroethanoic acid is the stronger of the two — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 2.59 against chloroethanoic acid's 2.86.

The Reason gives the cause exactly. Fluorine is the most electronegative element, more so than chlorine, so it withdraws electron density along the chain more strongly. That pull helps disperse the negative charge on the carboxylate ion left behind after the proton departs, and a more stable anion means the proton leaves more readily.

The effect follows electronegativity right down the group: fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo, in falling order of acid strength. It also falls off sharply with DISTANCE, being transmitted through bonds — 3-chlorobutanoic acid is markedly weaker than 2-chlorobutanoic acid.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(p\)-nitroaniline is a weaker base than \(p\)-toluidine.
Reason (R) : The electron donating \(-\,\mathrm{NO_2}\) group in \(p\)-nitroaniline makes it a weaker base.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

p-Nitroaniline IS the weaker base — its \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) is about 13 against p-toluidine's 8.9, a difference of four orders of magnitude. So the Assertion holds.

But the Reason describes the nitro group wrongly. A nitro group is strongly electron WITHDRAWING, not electron donating — it pulls density both inductively and by resonance, and from the para position it can draw the nitrogen's lone pair right onto its own oxygen.

That is exactly why the Assertion is true: a lone pair partly committed elsewhere is less available to accept a proton. The methyl group of p-toluidine does the opposite, releasing density towards the nitrogen and making that base stronger than aniline itself.

Corrected, the Reason would have explained the Assertion; as written it names the wrong effect.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}\mathrm{H}\) for an ideal solution is not equal to zero.
Reason (R) : A – B interactions in an ideal solution are same as between A – A and B – B interactions.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

For an IDEAL solution \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H\) IS equal to zero — that is part of the definition, along with \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}V = 0\) and obedience to Raoult's law over the whole range of composition. The Assertion denies it, so the Assertion is false.

The Reason is correct, and it is exactly WHY the enthalpy change is zero. Heat is absorbed or released on mixing only when the new A-B interactions differ in strength from the A-A and B-B interactions broken to make room for them. In an ideal solution the three are the same, so the energy balances exactly and no heat flows either way.

Benzene with toluene, and n-hexane with n-heptane, are the standard examples — pairs so alike chemically that a molecule of either barely notices which neighbour it has.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Separation of Zr and Hf is difficult.
Reason (R) : Zr and Hf are radioactive.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Zirconium and hafnium are genuinely difficult to separate, so the Assertion holds. But neither is RADIOACTIVE — both are ordinary stable elements, and radioactivity has nothing to do with the difficulty.

The real cause is LANTHANOID CONTRACTION. The fourteen lanthanoids come between them in the periodic table, and across that series the \(4f\) electrons shield the growing nuclear charge very poorly, so the radius shrinks steadily. That shrinkage very nearly cancels the increase the extra period would otherwise bring, leaving the two elements at almost exactly the same size — about 160 pm each.

Chemical separation depends on differences in size and in the properties that follow from it, so two elements of the same size in the same group behave almost identically.

rows.stem:
What happens when D-glucose is treated with the following reagents ?
(a) \(\mathrm{H_2N-OH}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\)
rows.solution:
(a) WITH HYDROXYLAMINE, D-glucose gives its OXIME. The nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon, water is lost, and a carbon-nitrogen double bond forms:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_2N{-}OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH({=}N{-}OH)(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is glucose oxime. That an ammonia derivative condenses with it at all is one of the proofs that glucose contains a CARBONYL group.

(b) WITH ACETIC ANHYDRIDE, glucose is acetylated to GLUCOSE PENTAACETATE:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{CHO(CH{-}OCOCH_3)_4CH_2{-}OCOCH_3}\)

Five acetyl groups go on, and each one requires a hydroxyl group to attach to — which is how the FIVE hydroxyl groups of glucose are counted. Together the two reactions establish one carbonyl and five hydroxyls, six of the molecule's functional positions.

rows.stem:
For a chemical reaction R \(\rightarrow\) P, the variation in the concentration [R] vs time t plot is given as :
(a) Predict the order of the reaction and write the unit of rate constant (k) for this order of reaction.
(b) What is the slope of the curve ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says the [R] vs t plot 'is given as :' and then PRINTS it, and the shape of that plot IS the answer to part (a), so it cannot be described. What can safely be said: a plain rectangular frame with a vertical axis labelled [R] carrying an upward arrow, a horizontal axis labelled t carrying a rightward arrow, NO tick marks and NO numbers anywhere on either axis, and a single plotted line running from near the top of the vertical axis down towards the lower right. The LINE'S SHAPE — the one property that discriminates the order, and therefore also part (b)'s answer — is deliberately WITHHELD. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(a) The plot of \([\mathrm{R}]\) against \(t\) is a STRAIGHT LINE that falls steadily. Only one order gives that shape.

For a zero order reaction \(\text{Rate} = k\), and integrating gives
\([\mathrm{R}] = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - kt\)
which is a straight line of intercept \([\mathrm{R}]_0\). Any other order would give a curve — first order decays exponentially, so a plot of concentration itself against time bends away and never reaches zero.

Order of the reaction: ZERO.

Unit of the rate constant: for order \(n\) the general form is \(\mathrm{mol^{1-n}\ L^{n-1}\ s^{-1}}\), and at \(n = 0\) that becomes
\(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)
the same units as rate itself — which is the signature of zero order and the reason the two are indistinguishable by their units.

(b) Comparing \([\mathrm{R}] = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - kt\) with \(y = c + mx\), the slope is
\(-k\)
negative, because the reactant is being consumed, so the rate constant is recovered as \(k = -\text{slope}\).

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the chemical equations when :
(a) Ethanal is treated with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine ?
(b) Propanone is treated with Zn(Hg) and conc. HCl ?
rows.solution:
(a) 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water, to give the 2,4-DINITROPHENYLHYDRAZONE:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{H_2N{-}NH{-}C_6H_3(NO_2)_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}N{-}NH{-}C_6H_3(NO_2)_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

This is Brady's reagent, and the reaction is a standard TEST: the product is an orange or red crystalline solid that appears at once, and its sharp melting point identifies which carbonyl compound it came from.

(b) Zinc amalgam with concentrated hydrochloric acid is CLEMMENSEN REDUCTION, which converts a carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\):
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{conc. }\mathrm{HCl}]{\mathrm{Zn(Hg)}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Propanone becomes propane. The carbon skeleton is untouched — only the oxygen goes. Wolff-Kishner reduction achieves the same conversion in ALKALI, and the choice between them is decided by what else in the molecule would survive the conditions.
